chapters.title: Chapter 2: Cyclical, Defensive, and Growth Sectors

lessons.title: Operating Leverage and Why Cyclicals Swing So Hard

body.text: A 20% fall in sales does not mean a 20% fall in profit. For a business with heavy fixed costs, it can wipe out most of the profit. For a business with mostly variable costs, profit falls roughly in line. Cost structure, not just demand, is what turns an economic slowdown into an earnings collapse.

children.text: The last lesson explained why cyclical sectors see demand swing with the economy. That is only half the story. Two companies can suffer the same drop in revenue and report completely different profit outcomes. The difference is operating leverage, and once you understand it you will read every 'margin expansion' and 'margin compression' headline differently.

columns.label: Fixed costs
points: Stay roughly the same whether you sell a lot or a little
Examples: depreciation on plants, permanent staff salaries, rent, aircraft lease rentals, network maintenance
Must be paid even in a bad quarter

columns.label: Variable costs
points: Rise and fall with every unit sold
Examples: raw materials, packaging, freight, sales commissions, fuel per flight

markDefs.definition: The extent to which a company's cost base is fixed rather than variable. High operating leverage means a small change in revenue causes a much larger percentage change in operating profit.

children.text: Once fixed costs are covered, almost every extra rupee of revenue drops straight to profit. When revenue falls, those fixed costs stay, and profit shrinks much faster than sales. The more of a company's cost base is fixed, the higher its

children.text: Two Companies, Same Profit, Different Risk

Take two illustrative companies with identical revenue of ₹1,000 crore and identical operating profit of ₹150 crore. On Screener.in, both would show a 15% operating margin. One is a cement maker with expensive plants. The other is a consumer goods company that outsources manufacturing. Their cost structures look nothing alike.

stats.context: A 1% change in revenue moves EBIT about 4%

stats.context: A 1% change in revenue moves EBIT about 1.67%

children.text: Now move revenue up and down by 20%. Variable costs move with revenue; fixed costs stay put. Company A: in a boom, revenue ₹1,200 crore minus variable costs ₹480 crore minus fixed ₹450 crore gives EBIT of ₹270 crore, up 80%. In a slump, ₹800 crore minus ₹320 crore minus ₹450 crore leaves just ₹30 crore, down 80%. Company B: in a boom, ₹1,200 crore minus ₹900 crore minus ₹100 crore gives ₹200 crore, up 33%. In a slump, ₹800 crore minus ₹600 crore minus ₹100 crore gives ₹100 crore, down 33%.

body.title: EBIT Under Three Revenue Scenarios (₹ crore)

body.text: Same starting margin, same revenue swing, but Company A's profit moves 80% while Company B's moves 33%. This is why cement, steel, airline, and hotel stocks can double or halve on a change in demand that looks modest in the revenue line.

body.title: Find Company A's Breakeven Revenue
body.prompt: Company A has fixed costs of ₹450 crore, and variable costs are 40% of revenue, so each rupee of revenue contributes 60 paise toward fixed costs. At what revenue does Company A's EBIT fall to exactly zero? Answer in ₹ crore.
body.explanation: Breakeven revenue = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution margin = ₹450 crore ÷ 0.60 = ₹750 crore. That is only 25% below the base year's ₹1,000 crore. For Company B, breakeven is ₹100 crore ÷ 0.25 = ₹400 crore, a 60% fall. Company A has far less room for a bad year.

children.text: Capacity Utilisation: Operating Leverage in Action

In manufacturing sectors, analysts talk about operating leverage through capacity utilisation. A plant's fixed costs are spread over however many units it actually produces. Run the plant harder and the fixed cost carried by each unit falls, lifting margins even if selling prices do not change.

body.latex: \text{Fixed cost per tonne} = \frac{\text{Annual fixed costs}}{\text{Tonnes produced}} \qquad \frac{\text{₹450 cr}}{\text{6 MT}} = \text{₹750} \qquad \frac{\text{₹450 cr}}{\text{8.5 MT}} \approx \text{₹529}
body.caption: A 10 million tonne cement plant with ₹450 crore of fixed costs, at 60% vs 85% utilisation

children.text: Moving from 60% to 85% utilisation cuts fixed cost per tonne from ₹750 to about ₹529, a saving of roughly ₹221 on every tonne before any price increase. This is why cement and steel management commentary obsesses over utilisation, and why analysts get excited when an industry's utilisation climbs toward 80% and above: pricing power and operating leverage tend to arrive together.

body.title: Spot the Highest Operating Leverage
body.question: Revenue falls 15% for each of these four businesses. Whose operating profit is likely to fall by the largest percentage?
options: A pharma distributor that buys and resells medicines
A hotel chain that owns its properties
A staffing company that pays contract workers only when clients use them
A commodity trading firm with a small office
body.explanation: A hotel that owns its properties carries heavy fixed costs: depreciation, maintenance, and permanent staff, which barely fall when occupancy drops. The distributor, staffing company, and trading firm have mostly variable costs that shrink along with revenue, so their profits fall roughly in proportion.

body.title: The Hotel Occupancy Recovery
body.scenario: A listed hotel company runs a 200-room property with an average room rate of ₹8,000 per night. Its fixed costs are ₹25 crore a year, and variable costs such as housekeeping supplies, laundry, and commissions are 20% of room revenue. Occupancy was 60% last year. Management says it expects 75% occupancy this year at the same room rate.
body.prompt: Estimate room revenue and EBITDA at both occupancy levels. By roughly what percentage does EBITDA grow compared with revenue? What does this tell you about headlines saying the stock 'looks expensive on last year's earnings'?
body.modelAnswer: Room nights available in a year: 200 × 365 = 73,000. At 60% occupancy: 43,800 room nights × ₹8,000 = ₹35.04 crore revenue. Variable costs at 20% = ₹7.01 crore. EBITDA = 35.04 - 7.01 - 25 = about ₹3.03 crore. At 75% occupancy: 54,750 room nights × ₹8,000 = ₹43.80 crore revenue. Variable costs = ₹8.76 crore. EBITDA = 43.80 - 8.76 - 25 = ₹10.04 crore. Revenue grows 25%, but EBITDA grows about 231%, more than tripling. A P/E based on last year's depressed earnings will look very high, but if the occupancy recovery is real, earnings can catch up very quickly. The flip side is the same maths in reverse: if occupancy slips back, profits vanish just as fast. Always ask how confident you are in the volume assumption.

body.title: Debt makes it worse: financial leverage on top of operating leverage

children.text: Interest is also a fixed cost, sitting below EBIT. Capital-heavy cyclicals often borrow to build their plants, so they stack financial leverage on top of operating leverage. Give both companies from our example ₹50 crore of annual interest and watch profit before tax.

content.caption: Profit Before Tax With ₹50 Crore Interest (₹ crore)

content.text: With debt added, a 20% revenue fall pushes Company A into a loss. This combination of high fixed costs and high debt is what turns ordinary cyclical downturns into balance sheet crises in sectors like steel, power, and infrastructure.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: A company with a high proportion of ___ costs will see its operating profit swing much more sharply than its revenue.
body.explanation: Fixed costs do not shrink when sales fall, so every rupee of lost revenue comes mostly out of profit. That is operating leverage.

body.title: Estimate Operating Leverage From an Annual Report
steps: Open the company's latest annual report or the Profit & Loss statement in its results filing on NSE or BSE
Identify costs that are mostly fixed: employee benefits expense, depreciation, and rent or lease-related costs
Identify costs that are mostly variable: cost of materials consumed, purchases of stock-in-trade, and freight
Divide the fixed cost total by revenue; a higher ratio suggests higher operating leverage
On Screener.in, check how much the operating profit margin (OPM %) moved in years when sales fell, such as the year ending March 2021
Compare with sector peers to see whether the company is more or less exposed than its industry

points: Operating leverage is the share of a company's costs that stay fixed as revenue changes
Degree of Operating Leverage (DOL) = Contribution ÷ EBIT; a DOL of 4 means a 1% revenue change moves EBIT about 4%
Two companies with the same revenue and margin can see very different profit swings; in the example, 80% vs 33% on a 20% revenue move
Capacity utilisation is operating leverage in manufacturing: higher utilisation spreads fixed costs over more units and lifts margins
Cement, steel, airlines, hotels, and telecom carry high operating leverage; FMCG, distributors, and trading businesses carry low operating leverage
Debt adds financial leverage on top, which can push a high fixed-cost cyclical from profit into loss in a modest downturn

body.text: All company figures in this lesson are illustrative and simplified for teaching. Real cost structures include semi-variable costs and change over time. Nothing here is an investment recommendation.
